historical_timeline.summary: Moves to Chicago and joins the Greater Salem Baptist Church.
First European tour, sung in pain with breathlessness, then cancelled; hysterectomy, with granulomas found and sarcoidosis diagnosed.
Sings at the March on Washington.
Admitted in Chicago after a coughing spell (month not recorded); told privately of a heart attack and sarcoidosis in her heart; a year of recovery without touring.
Cuts short a European tour; eye inflammation and cramps in her legs and hands.
Tours Japan, India and Europe; falls ill in Germany after her last concert, in Munich, and is hospitalized at home.
Dies at Little Company of Mary Hospital in Evergreen Park, Illinois, at 60.

claims.statement: Mahalia Jackson was born in New Orleans on October 26, 1911, the third of six children of a man who was a longshoreman by day, a barber by night and a clergyman on Sunday. Her mother died when she was six, and she was raised by an aunt in a poor but respectable home; she left school in the eighth grade to work as a cook and washerwoman.

source_links.locator: Born in New Orleans on Oct. 26, 1911, she was the third of six children; left motherless when she was 6; reared by Aunt Duke; obliged to leave school in the eighth grade to work as a cook and washerwoman
roster birth date

claims.statement: In 1928 she moved to Chicago, worked as a hotel maid and laundress, and joined the Greater Salem Baptist Church, where she became a soloist. She never learned to read music. After her Carnegie Hall debut on October 4, 1950, she began touring abroad in 1952, and toured widely for the rest of her life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her life as a touring singer anchors the modern social history and the plan built around her performing and travel.

source_links.locator: In 1928, she departed New Orleans for Chicago; Greater Salem Baptist Church; never learned to read music; Oct. 4, 1950, Carnegie Hall; began her tours abroad in 1952

claims.statement: She was closely associated with the civil rights movement and sang at the March on Washington in 1963 before Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s speech. When she moved into an all-white neighborhood on the South Side of Chicago, a bullet was fired through a window of her home.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern social history: a singer whose work was bound up with the civil rights movement, who met racist violence at home.

source_links.locator: chosen to sing at the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s March on Washington rally; a bullet was fired through a window of her home

claims.statement: Touring the segregated South for as many as 200 dates a year, she and her company had trouble finding safe places to sleep, eat and buy gas, sometimes slept in her car, lived on bags of fruit and drove half the night, and she arrived so exhausted she was almost dizzy when she sang; she insisted on being paid in cash because checks were often refused.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Context for the modern social history; the details come from a tertiary summary of her autobiography and Goreau's biography.

source_links.locator: performing 200 dates a year for ten years; difficulty finding safe, clean places to sleep, eat, and buy gas due to Jim Crow laws; living on bags of fresh fruit during the day and driving half the night; contracts demanded she be paid in cash
picked up the technique early after discovering that many segregated Southern banks wouldn't cash a check

claims.statement: Before and during her first European tour in 1952 she had difficulty breathing during and after performances and severe abdominal cramping, sang many shows in pain, lost a great deal of weight and finally cancelled the tour. On her return she had a hysterectomy, at which numerous granulomas were found in her abdomen, and she was diagnosed with sarcoidosis. From then on she had occasional bouts of fatigue and shortness of breath that became more frequent as her schedule filled.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern presenting problem and the past history. The account rests on Goreau's biography as summarized by Wikipedia and on TheWrap; no pathology record was found.

source_links.locator: she began having difficulty breathing during and after performances; had a hysterectomy and doctors found numerous granulomas in her abdomen. She was diagnosed with sarcoidosis; occasional bouts of fatigue and shortness of breath

claims.statement: In 1964, weeks after her marriage, she could not stop coughing on the drive home from a concert in St. Louis and admitted herself to a Chicago hospital. The diagnosis given in public was heart strain and exhaustion; her doctors told her privately that she had had a heart attack and that sarcoidosis was now in her heart. Recovery took a year, during which she could not tour or record and lost about 50 pounds; afterwards she had near-constant fatigue, bouts of tachycardia and high blood pressure. From 1964 she was in and out of hospitals, and physicians warned her of exhaustion from her itineraries.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented cardiac illness to which the modern diagnosis of cardiac sarcoidosis is linked. The account of what her doctors told her privately comes from Goreau's biography as summarized by Wikipedia.

claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective; the accounts conflict, and none gives a medical record. The modern episode does not resolve the question.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Diagnose and treat sarcoidosis with cardiac involvement in a 52-year-old Black woman and touring singer, in whom sarcoidosis is more common and more often severe and fatal than in White Americans, on the ATS 2020 diagnosis guideline, the ERS 2021 treatment guideline, the HRS 2014 cardiac sarcoidosis consensus and the AHA 2024 scientific statement: chest imaging with bilateral hilar adenopathy; pulmonary function with DLCO; EBUS-guided lymph node aspiration showing non-necrotizing granulomas, with tuberculosis and fungal infection excluded; screening every patient for other organ involvement (eye examination, ECG, calcium and vitamin D handling, liver and kidney tests); cardiac evaluation with ECG, Holter monitoring, echocardiography, cardiac MRI and FDG-PET before treatment begins; prednisone with methotrexate as a steroid-sparing agent, with methotrexate safety monitoring; bone protection that avoids calcium supplements while calcium is high; pneumocystis prophylaxis, vaccination and tuberculosis screening before immunosuppression; arrhythmia risk stratification with electrophysiology study and a defibrillator; and a plan that protects her voice, her performing and her travel.

visit_schedule.purpose: Three months of breathlessness, cough, tiredness and palpitations in a touring singer of 52: examination, chest radiograph, ECG and blood tests
EBUS result: sarcoidosis; pulmonology consultation, lung function, screening for other organ involvement, and cardiac tests
Cardiac MRI and FDG-PET results: cardiac sarcoidosis; start of prednisone and methotrexate, bone and infection protection, and electrophysiology referral
Nine weeks of treatment: lung function, calcium, methotrexate safety, the new defibrillator, steroid effects, and her concert schedule
Same-day sick visit for laryngitis on immunosuppressive treatment
Six months of treatment: repeat FDG-PET, steroid taper, and plans for touring

consultant_note.history: Ms. Jackson, 52, is seen at the request of Dr. Fontenot two weeks after she presented with three months of exertional breathlessness, dry cough, tiredness and palpitations. A CT of the chest two days later showed symmetric hilar and mediastinal adenopathy with perilymphatic upper-lobe nodules, and I performed EBUS-guided needle aspiration five days ago. She had a hysterectomy at 40, when granulomas were reported in her abdomen; no report survives. She stopped her calcium and vitamin D tablet two weeks ago. She has had one more spell of palpitations while singing; no fainting. She has postponed three weeks of concerts. She has no eye symptoms and no rash. Never smoker; no relevant exposures
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Fontenot's intake note and results. Chest radiograph: bilateral hilar adenopathy with upper-zone reticulonodular opacities (Scadding stage II). High-resolution CT: hilar, subcarinal and right paratracheal nodes up to 2.4 cm with fine calcification; perilymphatic micronodules in both upper lobes; no fibrosis. EBUS-guided aspiration of stations 4R, 7 and 11L: non-necrotizing granulomas; acid-fast and fungal stains negative; cultures pending; lavage lymphocytes 32 percent with a CD4 to CD8 ratio of 5.2. Interferon-gamma release assay and HIV negative. ECG: sinus rhythm, PR 240 ms, frequent unifocal ventricular ectopy. Pulmonary function today: FVC 74 percent, FEV1 76 percent, FEV1/FVC 80 percent, total lung capacity 78 percent, DLCO 62 percent of predicted. Calcium 10.7 mg/dL today off the supplement (10.8 at the first visit); creatinine 1.04 mg/dL; 25-hydroxyvitamin D 22 ng/mL; 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D 84 pg/mL; alkaline phosphatase 128 U/L; lymphocytes 0.9; NT-proBNP 210 pg/mL

assessment.display: Pulmonary sarcoidosis with lymph node involvement
assessment.assessment: Sarcoidosis is confirmed to the standard the ATS guideline asks: a compatible clinical and radiologic picture, non-necrotizing granulomas in lymph nodes obtained by EBUS rather than mediastinoscopy, and no evidence so far of tuberculosis, fungal infection or lymphoma, with final cultures to follow. The lavage lymphocytosis with a high CD4 to CD8 ratio supports it. It is Scadding stage II, with mild restriction and a reduced DLCO, and she is symptomatic. The granulomas reported at her abdominal operation are consistent with long-standing disease. Sarcoidosis is more common in Black women in the United States and carries a higher risk of severe and fatal disease, so a complete organ screen matters. Serum ACE adds nothing to the diagnosis and is not needed

Granulomas convert vitamin D to its active form, as the high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D with a low 25-hydroxyvitamin D shows. The supplement made it worse. No calcium or vitamin D supplements until the calcium is normal on treatment; then vitamin D may be replaced cautiously with calcium checks. Bone protection on glucocorticoids should use a bisphosphonate, not calcium tablets

assessment.display: Palpitations with first-degree atrioventricular block and ventricular ectopy
assessment.assessment: Unexplained conduction disease and ventricular ectopy in a patient with proven extracardiac sarcoidosis means cardiac sarcoidosis must be excluded. The HRS consensus and the AHA statement advise Holter monitoring, an echocardiogram, cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement and cardiac FDG-PET. The PET must be done before any glucocorticoid, which would mask active inflammation, and needs a 72-hour high-fat, very-low-carbohydrate preparation

recommendations: Complete the screen for other organ involvement: ophthalmology examination now and yearly; calcium, creatinine and liver tests at each visit; the ECG is done

Cardiac evaluation within two weeks and before any treatment: 24-hour Holter, echocardiogram, cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement, and cardiac FDG-PET with dietary preparation; joint review with cardiology

If cardiac sarcoidosis is confirmed: prednisone 40 mg daily for about two months, then a slow taper over about six months toward 5 to 10 mg, with methotrexate 15 mg weekly rising to 20 mg and folic acid, continued for at least a year; if the heart is not involved, the same steroid-sparing approach for symptomatic stage II disease with impaired lung function, at a lower prednisone dose

If cardiac sarcoidosis is confirmed with an ejection fraction above 35 percent, an electrophysiology study, and a dual-chamber defibrillator if sustained ventricular tachycardia is induced, given the conduction disease; a beta-blocker for the ventricular ectopy

Before immunosuppression: hepatitis B and C serology (drawn today), tuberculosis already excluded by the interferon-gamma release assay, and PCV20, recombinant zoster and, if non-immune, hepatitis B vaccines; no live vaccines on treatment

On treatment: pneumocystis prophylaxis with atovaquone while prednisone is 20 mg or more with methotrexate, avoiding trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; a bone density scan and a bisphosphonate; glucose, blood pressure, weight, sleep and mood checks; methotrexate blood tests every two to four weeks for three months, then every eight to twelve weeks; no alcohol
Response assessment: lung function about two months after starting and then every three to six months; repeat cardiac FDG-PET three to six months into treatment

Performing and travel: postpone concerts until the cardiac tests and any device implant are done, then resume a lighter schedule with rest days; voice care; carry a medicine list and any device card when travelling
